newsitem.title: ITALY: Mediaset unlikely to go for Olivetti.
newsitem.headline: Mediaset unlikely to go for Olivetti.

text.p: The chances of Italian television group Mediaset launching a full bid for ailing information technology group Olivetti are very slim, Mediaset Chief Executive Ubaldo Livolsi said.
A bid for Olivetti, which owns Italy's second mobile phone operator, Omnitel, would give Mediaset an immediate entry into the telecoms business.
Mediaset's preferred option is still to bid for a third licence when it comes up for auction next year.

"We are still considering this alternative (an Olivetti bid) but the chances are very limited because we don't think that in order to buy Omnitel we should really run the risk of buying the entire Olivetti business," Livolsi told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
"The first option ... is the bid for the third licence in the mobile business. That was the original idea and we still believe that is our best alternative," said Livolsi.
Mediaset has joined forces with Albacom, a joint venture between British Telecom and Banca Nazionale del Lavoro to bid for the third mobile phone licence next year.
Mediaset has weighed up the possibility of a bid for Olivetti because it would be the only way of securing the Omnitel business in the immedeiate future.
"For the next three years, according to the present law, Olivetti cannot sell the ownership of Omnitel," said Livolsi.
Another option that Mediaset has been looking at is whether to become a shareholder in state telecoms group Stet when it is privatised next year.
Stet owns a dominant stake in Italy's leading mobile phone player, Telecom Italia Mobile.

"We might consider being part of the consortium of shareholders who run the Stet business in the future. But that is also in terms of options and alternatives. We consider it a very low level of probability," said Livolsi.
Mediaset is also pondering a move into fixed line telecommunications in alliance with BT when the market is liberalised in 1998.
"That is the possibility we are considering and we would be pretty happy about that. It depends on the amount of investment which will be needed and the return on investment," said Livolsi.

Livolsi said he expected Mediaset's 1996 profits to be in line with analysts' forecasts and that 40 percent would be paid out in dividends. He added the company was on target to wipe out net financial debt by the end of the year.
